forces.title: Geopolitical Disruption to Critical Maritime Chokepoints
forces.description: The ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruption and intensifying Red Sea conflict highlight the severe vulnerability of global energy trade. Two-thirds of energy trade transits maritime chokepoints, making pipeline networks and LNG shipping vessels susceptible to widespread disruptions. These events create substantial uncertainty across energy markets, impacting supply routes and potentially undermining existing resilience mechanisms.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Increased Investment in Bypass Pipeline Infrastructure
forces.description: Countries and firms are actively investing in new pipelines to circumvent vulnerable chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz. These projects, such as Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline and ADNOC’s Fujairah pipeline, have already buffered significant oil supply shocks by moving additional crude. Further planned developments aim to create excess capacity and alternative routes, fundamentally reshaping midstream oil logistics and enhancing energy security.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Rewiring of Global Oil and LNG Trade Flows
forces.description: Geopolitical disruptions have led to a significant rewiring of global oil and LNG trade flows, with over one-fifth of seaborne oil trade re-routed in Q2 2026. This involves shifts in import/export patterns, with countries like China curtailing imports and the US increasing exports. This trend impacts demand for specific shipping routes, port infrastructure, and the operational flexibility required for LNG shipping vessels and crude/product storage terminals.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Depletion of Strategic Oil Inventories and Refining Strain
forces.description: The drawing down of strategic petroleum reserves (e.g., US SPR to historical lows) and the strain on the global refining system pose a significant risk. Refined product inventories are thinner and more fragmented than crude stocks, leading to localized scarcity. This could trigger more efforts to shore up refined product buffers, impacting storage terminal utilization and investment decisions within the midstream sector.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: LNG Buyers Prioritizing Geographic Diversification of Supply
forces.description: LNG buyers across Europe are increasingly prioritizing geographic diversification of supply in their procurement strategies. This structural shift, driven by recent transit disruptions, aims to mitigate supply risks and enhance resilience. It implies a demand for new LNG suppliers, flexible contractual terms, and potentially new LNG shipping routes and receiving terminals to accommodate a broader range of import sources.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Increased Investment in LNG Resilience Infrastructure
forces.description: Companies are planning increased investment in LNG supply resilience measures, including storage infrastructure, LNG shipping vessels, floating storage and regasification units (FSRUs), regasification terminals, and interconnectors. This proactive approach by buyers, including those in Europe, represents a significant upside for the midstream sector, driving demand for new capacity and upgrades to existing infrastructure to manage future disruptions and volatility.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: LNG Procurement Shifts to Prioritize Security Over Cost Minimization
forces.description: The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz is causing a structural shift in LNG procurement strategies, with a move from cost minimization to prioritizing security of supply. This change in emphasis affects how LNG shipping contracts are structured, the willingness to invest in diverse supply sources, and the demand for flexible midstream solutions, ultimately reshaping the competitive landscape and investment rationale for LNG transport and storage.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Concentrated Global LNG Supply Chains Pose Resilience Risk
forces.description: Over 62% of internationally traded LNG originated from just three countries in 2025, creating concentrated supply chains that pose a significant resilience risk, particularly for Europe. This dependency on a limited number of sources for LNG supply means that disruptions in any of these countries could have widespread impacts on LNG shipping, regasification terminals, and regional gas supply, challenging Europe's energy security.
forces.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

forces.title: High Import Dependence Exposes Irish Energy Sector to Price Volatility
forces.description: Ireland's energy sector, including its gas transmission and distribution, faces significant risk from high import dependence (approximately 80%) and continued reliance on fossil fuels, particularly gas. This exposure to global energy price volatility and geopolitical shocks directly impacts the operational costs and profitability of midstream operators, who must manage procurement strategies and customer pricing to absorb cost increases.

forces.title: Regulated Revenue Streams Insulate State-Backed Gas Infrastructure Operators
forces.description: State-backed operators in Ireland's energy sector, such as GNI (Gas Networks Ireland), benefit from relatively insulated positions due to regulated revenue streams. This provides a degree of stability and protection against the volatile energy market conditions. Such regulatory frameworks support ongoing investment in gas transmission and distribution infrastructure, ensuring long-term stability for these midstream assets.

forces.title: Strengthening Contractual Protections for LNG Supply
forces.description: In response to increased disruption risk, over half of LNG buyers plan to strengthen contractual protections in the next 2-3 years. Top priorities include force majeure clauses, delivery terms, volume flexibility, and pricing clauses. This indicates a structural shift in commercial models for LNG supply agreements, aiming to enhance legal protection and manage risks for both buyers and LNG shipping/terminal operators.
forces.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

forces.title: Discussions on New Oil and Gas Capacity in Norway
forces.description: Norway is discussing plans for new oil and gas capacity. If realized, this could represent an upside driver for the midstream sector, requiring investment in new or expanded pipeline networks and storage facilities to transport the additional output to markets. Such developments would enhance energy security for Europe and reinforce Norway's role as a key energy supplier.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: Energy system resilient to Hormuz shock, but long-term vulnerabilities persist for global supply
viewpoints.description: The global energy system, including oil and LNG flows, has shown more resilience than expected during the Strait of Hormuz disruption due to temporary buffers like bypass pipelines and strategic inventories. However, this resilience has limits, with inventories thinning and refining systems stressed. The crisis exposes lingering vulnerabilities, highlighting the need for structural changes beyond short-term measures to manage future supply shocks effectively.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: New bypass pipelines and LNG infrastructure to offset Strait of Hormuz disruption
viewpoints.description: Measures under discussion or already underway, such as building additional pipelines to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz and advancing LNG export/import infrastructure (including in the EU), could offset 35-70% of precrisis oil flows by 2030 in the event of future shocks. While implementation takes time and money, these efforts offer substantial results in managing vulnerabilities, creating optionality for energy flows.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: LNG buyers anticipate structural shifts in procurement strategies post-Strait of Hormuz disruption
viewpoints.description: Approximately 80% of LNG buyers, including those in Europe, expect changes in their procurement strategies due to the Strait of Hormuz disruption, with nearly half anticipating structural shifts. This indicates a move away from pure cost minimization towards prioritizing security of supply. The sentiment suggests a recognition that geopolitical conflicts and supply chain disruptions may become more frequent, necessitating fundamental adjustments.
viewpoints.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

viewpoints.title: Geographic diversification and flexibility become top priorities for LNG procurement in Europe
viewpoints.description: In response to transit disruptions, 80% of European LNG buyers plan to increase suppliers and geographic diversification in the next 2-3 years, making it the most common strategic change. Greater flexibility, portfolio optimization, and contractual protections are also high priorities. This signals a proactive approach to mitigating future supply risks and enhancing the resilience of LNG supply chains.
viewpoints.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

viewpoints.title: LNG buyers increasing investment in resilience measures, particularly storage and shipping
viewpoints.description: Approximately 66% of LNG buyers, including those in Europe, are planning to increase investment in resilience measures. Key areas of focus include storage infrastructure (30% of respondents), shipping (19%), floating storage and regasification units (FSRUs, 15%), regasification capacity (13%), and interconnectors (6%). These investments aim to manage disruption and volatility, indicating a strengthening of midstream LNG assets.
viewpoints.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

viewpoints.title: Concentrated LNG supply chains pose significant resilience risk for Europe
viewpoints.description: The energy system faces resilience risks due to concentrated supply chains. In 2025, over 62% of internationally traded LNG originated from just three countries (Australia, Qatar, US), posing a significant gas-dependency challenge for Europe. This concentration creates vulnerabilities that could impact affordability and reliability, even potentially exceeding the resilience risks associated with low-carbon technologies.
viewpoints.source_title: Investing in the energy transition: Time to look at whole-system value

viewpoints.title: Ireland's energy sector exposed to price volatility and geopolitical shocks due to import dependence
viewpoints.description: Ireland's energy sector, including its gas infrastructure, faces significant exposure to price volatility, geopolitical energy shocks, and grid constraints due to its approximately 80% import dependence and continued reliance on fossil fuels, particularly gas. While state-backed operators like GNI benefit from regulated revenue streams, oil-exposed operators face considerable pressure, influencing near-term performance based on energy prices and infrastructure capacity.

viewpoints.title: LNG buyers require enhanced capabilities for managing market volatility and supply disruption
viewpoints.description: While 75-85% of LNG buyers feel relatively confident in their trading and risk management capabilities, only 25-28% consider them fully sufficient for the current level of market volatility. This highlights a capability gap that needs to be addressed through improvement and upskilling, especially for European buyers navigating complex and volatile operating environments exacerbated by geopolitical disruptions to transit routes.
viewpoints.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement

demand_drivers.description: The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz created an urgent need to reroute oil flows to ensure supply continuity, driving the utilization of alternative pipeline capacity.

market_sizing.methodology: Incremental crude oil volumes moved around the Strait of Hormuz during Q2 2026 (relative to Q4 2025) via Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline and ADNOC’s pipeline to Fujairah. This represents a significant rerouting capacity for crude oil.
market_sizing.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

demand_drivers.description: The need to reduce reliance on vulnerable chokepoints and build resilience against future supply disruptions drives the demand for new pipeline infrastructure.

new_opportunities.description: Development of additional pipeline infrastructure offers substantial opportunities to create optionality for oil flows and enhance energy security for economies dependent on Gulf supply.

market_sizing.methodology: Measures under discussion or already underway, specifically new pipelines to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz, are estimated to offset between 35% and 70% of precrisis oil flows through the Strait by 2030 in the event of a future shock. This range is dependent on the translation of discussions into realized projects.
market_sizing.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

demand_drivers.description: The cascading effects of geopolitical events like the Strait of Hormuz disruption heighten awareness of supply chain vulnerabilities, prompting investment in resilience.

new_opportunities.description: 30% of surveyed LNG buyers plan to invest in storage infrastructure to enhance supply security.
19% of surveyed LNG buyers plan to invest in shipping to diversify and secure transport routes.
15% of surveyed buyers plan to invest in Floating Storage and Regasification Units (FSRUs), and 13% in regasification terminals, to increase import flexibility and capacity.
6% of surveyed buyers plan to invest in interconnectors to improve gas grid flexibility and regional supply integration.

market_sizing.methodology: Based on a pulse survey of 30 LNG buyers (including Europe) conducted in April 2026. 66% of respondents indicated their companies are planning to increase investment in resilience measures.
market_sizing.source_title: LNG buyers’ sentiment: Disruption and implications for procurement
